title: Three Ways to Stoke the Value Fireplace
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Using a fireplace metaphor prompted by cold January weather, Dave Stuart Jr. lays out three angles teachers can use to build the Value belief in their classrooms — the sense students need that a subject is genuinely worthwhile, not just a hoop to jump through. The Teacher Angle calls for talking to students more frequently, creatively, and confidently about why the work matters, cautioning against over-relying on utility and relevance arguments and pointing instead toward Mini-Sermons and the 'Rainbow of Why' framework, illustrated with a physics teacher's comment that the framework is really about deeper motivational layers, not just surface-level application. The Student Angle shifts the work onto students themselves, asking them to articulate a subject's value through Valued Within exercises like the Utility-Value T-Chart, Why Conversations, Mathy Moments, and end-of-unit Pop-Up Debates. The Class Angle, which Stuart says only became clear to him while building his Value Belief Mini-Course, locates value-building in the actual design of lessons and knowledge-building opportunities themselves, not just in what teachers or students say about the subject. Together the three angles map onto Strategies #4, #5, and #6 of The Will to Learn.
points: The three-angle framework (Teacher, Student, Class) gives teachers a structural map for Value-belief-building rather than treating 'make it relevant' as the only lever available.
The Teacher Angle explicitly warns against over-relying on utility and relevance arguments, redirecting teachers toward Mini-Sermons and the deeper motivational layers captured in the Rainbow of Why.

A physics teacher's own words — that the Rainbow of Why framework is 'actually about the bottom,' not the surface-level top — reinforce that Value-building works better through deeper meaning than through practical application alone.
The Student Angle reframes Value-building as something students must actively articulate themselves through structured Valued Within exercises, not something teachers merely assert to them.

Stuart's admission that the Class Angle only became clear to him while building a later course shows an author revising his own framework in public rather than presenting it as finished from the start.
quotes: So in our classrooms, there's a thing that's kind of got that some soul-warming power: the Value belief.

When most of the room is on the path to knowing in their hearts that math or science or social studies or writing are special, powerful, freeing, expanding, meaningful, I'm positive that, if we just had the right kind of glasses, we'd see the room aglow.

Most of us don't talk to our students frequently or creatively or winsomely or confidently enough about why we think the work of learning in our class is worthwhile. And even when we do this, we focus way too often on utility and relevance.
Just love the Rainbow of Why because when you are teaching something like physics people think it's about the top but it's actually about the bottom.
Another thing we don't do enough is genuinely ask and expect our students to explain how what they're learning is Valuable.
Through the work we give students to do, the lessons we teach, the opportunities to build knowledge we provide, we're doing a lot more Value heavy lifting than we may realize.
